utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Is the Prosecution ready to resume the cross-examination of Witness DP2?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think we've -- oh, no, we'll first perhaps deal with the documents of last week. That would be a better idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness Indic has written down the name of one of the interpreters. It has been spelled out and it appears rightly in the last transcript. So, therefore, there's no need to formally mark for identification the small note the witness prepared in that respect. Madam Registrar, apart from that irrelevant document, could you guide us through the relevant ones.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D184, transcript of interview conducted in Sarajevo, 28 February to 1 March 2000; D453 and 453.1, regular combat report with situation in 1600 hours for VRS main staff and forwarded command post, re UNPROFOR activities 04/02/94; D560 and D560.1, regular combat report with the situation at 1700 for VRS main staff, re activity of UNPROFOR 30/03/94; D561 and D561.1, regular combat report with the situation at 1700 for VRS main staff, re activities of UNPROFOR 31/03/94; D1656 and D1656.1, regular combat report with the situation at 1800 for VRS main staff, re UNPROFOR organised a meeting of mixed group 05/11/92; D1655, D1655.1, regular combat report with situation at 1400 for VRS staff, meeting of mixed group in organisation of UNPROFOR, 05/11/92; D1839, D1839.1, order of the main staff forwarded to all subordinate corps, the document dated 6 August 1993 regarding the movement of UNPROFOR and humanitarian aid convoys; D1840, D1840.1, protest that was sent by SRK command and UNPROFOR command regarding the violation of the cease-fire, 21 April 1994; D467 and D467.1, regular combat military report with situation at 1700 for VRS main staff, re units respecting signed truce, 21/02/94; P3777, order Sarajevo Romanija Corps command dated 29/01/1993; P3777.1, English translation; P3449A, photograph; P3778, report dated 04/02/94.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have noticed that the cassette that we wanted to tender hasn't been mentioned in this list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The video cassette, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The video that we saw, that we watched last Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has a copy been provided -- we have seen it, but having provided the copy to -- or is it still in the technical booth, or where did it go?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I assume that it's still in the technical booth because the hearing of Mr. Indic hadn't been completed. But I think it's in the other courtroom, so I don't know where it is actually located, where this cassette is actually located now. It was in the hands of the technicians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then deal with it after the break and try to find out where the cassette is. Since I did not hear any objections, the document as listed by --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In relation to the -- the videotape and the transcript of interview, I maintain my objection that I made at the time that the Defence sought to show it. In relation to the various combat reports, the Prosecution takes its usual stance, that only those parts which are the subject of evidence should be tendered. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think we heard the objections against the video already before and we have taken a decision on that and it was introduced perhaps in a bit different way from what the Defence had in mind. But we'll take a decision on that as soon as the video has been retrieved and the other reports admitted to the extent that they are the subject of examination of the witness and to the extent that they have been translated. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think Mr. Ierace addressed me. But is there -- is it a new issue you want to deal with, or is it something on the -- Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if I may. With regard to the document, the Defence would like to point out that it's obvious that these documents always have stamps, and in certain cases signatures. And naturally the authenticity of the document can't be contested. So even if the documents haven't always been translated, the Defence has no comment to make with regard to these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When you say the -- "naturally the authenticity of the documents can't be contested," do I have to understood that it is the position of the Defence that if a photocopy of a document bearing a stamp is there, that the authenticity is on from that moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. I said that it can't be -- well, it can always be contested, but less and less so to the extent that the witness has recognised the document as being a document the origin of which is in the corps or in a certain part of the army, et cetera. That's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it's not necessary, you would say, to have the testimony of the person who signed himself or who put the stamp himself. That's not necessary to establish the authenticity of the document. I do understand the position of the Defence. Then Mr. Ierace, you wanted to raise the next issue, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. On Friday and today, there have been some filings in these proceedings and some correspondence, in particular in relation to two issues: Whether the accused gives evidence; and secondly, matters to do with the expert witnesses. The Prosecution could respond in writing by way of a filing. Alternatively, given that both issues are very pressing, if I could be given a few minutes either later in this session or at the outset tomorrow, I could respond orally, which perhaps would save some time. But there are a number of issues which require immediate -- an immediate response. To give an example, I note that the Defence has still not provided a list of exhibits or a time estimate for the testimony of General Galic should he give evidence, and we're still waiting on some translations of annexes. So Mr. President, the matter for the Trial Chamber is to whether you would prefer me to proceed orally or in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is willing to hear whatever observations you would like to make in respect of the filings at this very moment, Mr. -- But if you would prefer to do it later this afternoon, it's fine as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I would, Mr. President. I've received some correspondence in the last few minutes. So perhaps at the beginning of the next -- at the beginning of the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll do it then. Then -- but now ten minutes later, is the Prosecution still ready to resume the examination of Witness DP2?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I'm well informed that the witness was protected by facial distortion and by pseudonym would be Witness DP2. That means that we have to pull the curtains down when he enters the courtroom. Mr. Usher, perhaps with the assistance of -- I -- that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, before I start, if I may have some indication as to how much time I'm left with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as my recollection goes, you took approximately some 40 minutes, I think, on the 11th of December. But I just asked Madam Registrar to inform me about the time the examination-in-chief took.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, it's 1 hour and 15 minutes, a bit more -- 1 hour 20 minutes left for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon and welcome back, Mr. DP2. May I remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, early December 2002.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And I'm glad to be here again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, I think that the curtains may be pulled up again. The counsel for the Prosecution will now resume its cross-examination, Mr. DP2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I proceed, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: On the previous day you testified that a friend of yours - and I will not mention his name, because you provided us with the name under protective measures - that this friend informed you that the two mortars located in front of the kindergarten which you marked with -- marked the map with figure "2" and the two mortars located in front of the Winter Olympics museum, which you marked with figure "3" were destroyed by shells fired from the Serb side. And I'm referring to evidence in transcript page number 17161.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was what I said. That was at the beginning of May 1982 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You were informed of this when, sir? When did your friend inform of this? Perhaps if you could give the month and the year.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we saw each other two months later. So if that was in May, then he told me about this in June -- July.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You said 1982, if I heard you right. Is it 1982 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So you were informed by this friend that they were destroyed in -- you were informed of this by your friend in June 1992. That is your testimony.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In view of that, sir, how do you explain your previous testimony -- and I'm referring to transcript page number 17189 -- that you saw two mortars at each of these locations in the period December 1992 to January 1993? Because your testimony is that in June 1992 your friend informed that they were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. Those mortars which fired on the Serbian side, they were destroyed and the kindergarten was set on fire, and in December 1992 or January 1993 at the same location I only saw two mortars.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, permit me to remind you. Your testimony was that -- if I may read your own words to you, transcript page number 17161. In reference to the mortars located in front of the kindergarten and the Winter Olympics museum which you marked on the map, you stated: "I didn't hear, but a friend who lives near these two checkpoints, near these two locations, these two sites of mortars, he told me that these two places were hit from the Serb side and that these four mortars were destroyed." Your testimony was referring to those mortars. You were referring to those particular mortars. You said that your friend referred to they were destroyed. Now you're contradicting yourself, I put it to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with what you have read out. That is how it was and that is what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you that your testimony with regard to mortars being present at location marked by you as number 2 and number 3 is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: So you're saying that in December or January 1992/1993 I didn't see --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if one wants to refer to numbers 2 and 3, I think it would be reasonable to show the witness the map again, because I myself no longer know where number 2 and number 3 were located.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne is entitled to do so, but it's not the exact location that counts but the possible contradiction where the witness referred to, as Ms. Mahindaratne puts it to him, to the same mortars he indicated on the map. And I think it's not necessary to do that. But of course Ms. Mahindaratne is allowed to do it. Ms. Mahindaratne is asking you for a comment on her understanding of your testimony, that is, that you heard from a friend that the mortars you indicated on the map -- and she has been talking about mortars in front of the kindergarten and mortars in front of the Olympic museum -- were already destroyed prior to the time you said you saw them at these same locations. Could you please try to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I certainly couldn't have seen the same mortars if they'd already been destroyed. I saw some other mortars several months later at the same two locations. And with your permission, Your Honours, last time I described those places I made an effort and three or four days ago I made some photographs of those two locations. So I can show the photographs too. I promise to bring them to this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I can show them to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Usually if any photographs are introduced, it's done by the parties. So if you would offer these to the parties, these photographs for inspection, then the parties could decide whether or not they would like you to -- whether they would like to tender these photographs in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That won't be necessary, Mr. President. I will move on to another area from here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, because you spoke of the parties, because we haven't been in touch with this witness obviously. Could Mr. Usher let us have a look at the photographs, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps first they should be shown to the Chamber so that we know what the witness is offering to the parties. Mr. Usher, could you please receive the photographs from the ... May I just ask you: I take it that you took these photographs because of the locations being shown on it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And these photographs will corroborate my description of the location where I saw the mortars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what you -- that's what you expect. The photographs showing locations are, as far as I understand, you put them at the disposal of the parties to see whether it will be of any use for them to use them in evidence. They may be given to the Defence and to the Prosecution. I take it that you'll have a look at it and then see whether it could assist you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I proceed in the meanwhile, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I proceed in the meanwhile?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed meanwhile.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, when I questioned you about the description of the Winter Olympics museum at which you claim you saw two mortars, you described it as a building with three storeys. Is it your position that at the time you saw -- you claim you saw these mortars, the building consisted of three storeys?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was the building intact at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not intact. It had damage. It's damaged today, and it's possible to see it on the photograph. It has not been renovated.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Wasn't it the case, sir, that this museum was in fact very badly damaged to the point of destruction in April 1992 due to shell fire and it has been repaired since, much later, after the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The museum must have been hit in May, not in April 1992. And the building looks very much the same as it did then. It was damaged and it's damaged today.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May the witness be shown a map bearing -- it's number D1817.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, you marked Markale market on this map, south of the locations marked as "2" and "3," the blue circle.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you testified that Markale market is located on Marsal Tito Street.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can the map be placed on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. DP2, could you leave the map on the ELMO so that we also can see it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I suggest to you, sir, that Markale market is not located on Marsal Tito Street but is located on the street referred to as Mula Mustafe Baseskije Street, which is the street joining Marsal Tito Street on the east end of Marsal Tito Street, that is, to the -- or further east of the location you marked as Markale market. Could you please place your pointer on the position you marked as Markale market.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we, please, zoom in on the specific location of the --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you take your pointer further east to the position where number "101" is, I suggest to you, sir, that Markale market is in fact located on Mula Mustafe Baseskija Street under the number 101, very near the cathedral, which is about -- would be about 300 metres to the east of the location you marked.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's incredible that having lived in Sarajevo for 40 years, I now have to show and demonstrate to the Trial Chamber how much you are in error and how much you are mistaken. The church is very far away from Markale, and Markale is located next to the rail, the tram rails of Tito street. It is true that it's called Mula Mustafe Baseskija, but here you can see Marsala Tito Street, and the last "T" is exactly located in relation to the Markale market, and that has always been Marsala Tito Street and it's called that today. And these two mortars were 100 to 150 metres as the crow flies. And if you show me those two photographs that I took, I would tell you that it's exactly behind the building of that part of the staircase where the Markale market is located. I think you're wasting your time. You're trying to convince me where Markale is located.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. DP2, there's no reason to tell any counsel whether Prosecution of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... In that time. Ms. Mahindaratne, may I ask you is there any dispute between the parties where the Markale market is?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. My question -- point was that this witness claimed that Markale market was his point of reference in identifying other locations and...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say he marked it wrongly on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I will move on now. I don't intend to stay on this point any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, you testified that the kindergarten in front of which you claimed to see two mortars, which is now the Embassy of the Holy See, was located on a street called Logavina Street, and I'm referring to transcript page 17191. And I suggest to you -- and I suggest to you, witness, that that is incorrect and the Embassy of the Holy See is in fact located on the a street named -- I will spell it to you since my pronunciation of it will be bad. P-e-h-l-i -- P-e-h-l-i-b-a-n-s with a full diacritic and A. P-e-h-l-i-b-a-n-s-a Street.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, well, I apologise for what I said earlier. But now I'm going to tell you that you're in the right. I made a mistake. That's not the street. It's the street that before the war was called Vuka Karadzica Street. And I hope you will forgive me. I have made a mistake with these two streets. And now I presume that this is the new name for this street. But before the war, it was called Vuka Karadzica Street.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, you testified that you saw on 28th October 1993, at the location you marked with figure "4" the number of weapons, which was the headquarters you claimed were of -- was the headquarters of Caco and his unit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the 10th Mountain Brigade of the commander Musan Topalovic, also known as Caco. And Your Honours, you can have a look at the photograph. I took it. That's where the staff was --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you due to time restraint. If you -- that was your evidence, in fact, that you saw this on the 28th of October, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd just like to change the date because in my diary, which I have in Sarajevo, I said the 28th, but it's true that that was on the 26th of October. The 26th of October, that's when Caco died. Not on the 28th but on the 26th. And I saw that in the afternoon, sometime about 1900 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was that the only day or the only time you saw this, at that particular location, or did you have the opportunity to see these weapons at that location either prior to that day or after that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained last time as well that I saw that in the course of an inter-Muslim conflict, when myself, my wife, and 50 or 60 other people --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you. Just a yes or no will suffice. Did you happen to see these weapons either before or after that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that room where I was a hostage, only on that day. I couldn't have seen it any other day because that was in his main staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you describe what this location was like. Was it just a room, or was it a particular building? A brief description would suffice.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give you a brief description while the photograph is there for you to have a look at it. It was just next to the building of the military command. It used to be of the Yugoslav People's Army. And in the war that's where the SFOR was located, the unit of the Egyptian Army. It's a ground-floor building. We, the hostages, were in a large building which could have been a dining hall, and when we left, in the second building, as we were leaving, and also in another room I saw all those weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please have the microphone adjusted, the microphone put closer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The photograph is with the Defence, and you can have a look at the building. It is more of a prefabricated building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. DP2, there's no need to refer to photographs until the parties have decided to pay attention to these photographs and tender them into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is it your position, sir, that the Egyptian SFOR was also located in the same building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the same building. The Egyptian forces were located in the former military building. It's a very large building. And next to that building, 10 metres from there, was the staff of the 10th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So your position is that the Egyptian SFOR was located just 10 metres from this particular location, which you have marked as number 4.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You testified that you'd been to the brewery, which you marked on the map with figure "5."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We brought water there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: How many times have you visited this location, during the period you were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say every day. Sometimes once; sometimes twice.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: According to your own testimony, you never saw any weapons or indications of production of weapons at the brewery, and you only heard rumours to such effect.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't see. I only heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your testimony was that these rumours were confirmed, at least to you, by what you saw and marked with figure "6" and that you saw two men testing weapons at the location you marked with figure "6"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What is the distance between location 5 and location 6?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the brewery and that place?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as the crow flies, about 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You testified that you saw three or four tanks below the Ciglane tunnel and near the engineering and architecture faculty.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You marked those two locations with figures "7" and "8."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: How many tanks did you see at the tunnel, at the location you marked with figure 8, that is, the east end of the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One tank.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And how many tanks did you see at the -- at least near the faculties?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two. Two.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When did you see the tanks near the tunnel? At least if you can give a month and a year.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw these tunnels often and any citizen of Sarajevo that happened on that market or was moving towards the hospital would be able to see these tanks. I saw the tanks from about mid-1992 until I left Sarajevo, which was the 9th of June, 1994. They were hidden by these two buildings, and that's where they moved.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In reference to the tanks near the faculties, was it during the same period that you saw the tanks there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which period of time?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When you said "mid-1992 to June 1994," you saw these tanks, are you saying you saw these tanks near the faculty buildings during the same period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not during the same time. Sometimes I wouldn't see the tank in the tunnel. It was probably inside. But regularly between the faculty buildings, I would be able to see the tank.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, you marked the position you claim you saw the tanks near the faculties with figure 7. Can you please examine the map again. And I'm referring to the location marked with figure "7." That's the tunnel. I'm referring to the faculties.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 7 is the tunnel. And here below in this faculty, from 8 towards the tunnel, that's where I saw the tanks. Here and here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we please zoom in on the part of the map the witness is pointing at. Would you please move it so, Mr. Usher, that we can see the relevant part. If the map could be pulled down once a bit. Yes. Yes, that's sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, what is the place you marked with number "8"? Could you describe that place, the position marked with figure 8. What is that place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 8, I marked the place -- the location in the tunnel where the tank would be. It's true I didn't mark it properly. It should be marked as the entrance to the tunnel. I don't know why I marked it there. I probably didn't see it well. But that is the location.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you claimed that you all saw tanks at the faculties, which you marked with figure "7." Could you please place your pointer on figure 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, before we continue, could I just verify that Mr. DP2, when you said your marking of number 8 was not correct, did you then point at the western entrance of the tunnel as the right location? Would you please point again at where you saw the tank.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness is now pointing to the western entry of the tunnel rather than the eastern entry of the tunnel where he made the marking number 8. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, drawing your attention to the position marked 7. Now, you claim that you saw tanks near the faculties which you said you would mark or which you marked with figure "7."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I suggest to you, Witness, that the position you marked with figure 7 is in fact a building belonging to the Kosevo hospital complex.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the hospital complex of Kosevo, but between the student clinic, outpatient clinic, and the engineering architectural faculty.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, your testimony was that you saw tanks at the location marked 7. Isn't that the case? That was your testimony.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your testimony was that you saw tanks at the location you marked with figure "7." That was your testimony. Or are you withdrawing that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't withdraw that. I can believe that precise location where I've put it on the map may not be perfectly good, but my description is good, what I've said about it being located between the students' outpatients clinic and engineering architectural faculty. That's where the two tanks were.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, your testimony was - and I will read you testimony back to you - at transcript page number 17169. You were asked, "How many have you seen," referring to tanks. "Three or four." "Where?" "Below the tunnel of Ciglane and near the engineering school, engineering faculty and architecture faculty." That was your testimony. Now, that was the location you marked with figure "7."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And I put it to you that the location you have marked with figure "7" is not -- you do not find faculties there. It is in fact a building, to be precise the traumatology department of the Kosevo hospital, it is within the Kosevo hospital complex. That's where you have marked with figure "7."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that it's possibly that I didn't mark it properly. But what I've told you, the description, you can read the description, and that told that between the outpatients' clinic and the architectural faculty. I can allow for the position that I've marked isn't proper, but my description is correct. I didn't say that I saw the tanks in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, is it your position then that you are not too familiar with this map you marked? That it's quite possible that you have -- your markings may not be accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not accurate because the streets have changed their names, and I really found it very difficult to find my bearings on this map. But now I can have a look at it again and mark it properly and accurately.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, for somebody who, by your own claim, has lived in Sarajevo for quite a long time, is it your position that you cannot recognise the Kosevo hospital complex on a map as simple as this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the map in front of me is clear, but the one here, I couldn't find my bearings. But I'm saying that I'm telling the truth, and it was like I said. I know Sarajevo very well, and I really didn't say that the tanks were in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You did not say it, but in marking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, isn't it clear that the marking -- the witness admitted that now two, three, or four times, that the markings are not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. I'll move --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It wouldn't be of any use to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, I appreciate that in view of your own testimony, that your markings are incorrect. But the other markings on this map made by you are also unreliable?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to point this out to me on the map so that I can see it. They are not incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: During this period that you saw these tanks, Witness, did you ever see the tanks fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. But I heard that fire was opened from tanks and that the tank at the entrance to the tunnel had been hit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Moving on to another area. You testified that you had seen mortars placed in vehicles in Sarajevo. I'm referring to testimony on page number 17149.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You described these vehicles as a van with a flatbed, a platform at the back.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you describe it further. Was it exposed on the three sides, the platform, or were there -- were the sides raised above the platform? Do you understand what I'm saying? What I'm asking is were there covers on the three sides of the platform or was it a flat open platform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There weren't any sides. That's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you personally see these vehicles, or is it based on rumours that you testified to this fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally saw those vehicles on many occasions. And all the inhabitants of Sarajevo who were objective will confirm this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: How many times did you see such vehicles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twenty-odd times.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you please perhaps give the period during which you saw these vehicles, perhaps the month and the year.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not just the month and the year. I'll give you the time period. The end of 1992 up until the first half of 1994, as far as I could follow everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Where were you when you saw these vehicles? Was it just walking by -- on the street? Did the vehicles pass you? Or how did you see these vehicles? What were the circumstances under which you saw these vehicles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On about five occasions I saw fire being opened, so I had to run to take shelter in my flat. But all the other ones were ones that I saw when I was going -- when I was passing by, when I was going to perform my work obligations. And it was not just myself who saw this. In all parts of town, when speaking to my friends, they all claimed that there were such vehicles, in Novo Sarajevo as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you perhaps name some of the streets on which you saw these vehicles. Perhaps specify the locations.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Bistricka Street, and the street from the post office. I don't exactly know the name. I don't know the exact name, but it was near the fish restaurant -- the seafood restaurant. And then it went upwards. That's where I personally saw those two tanks. And in the Vuka Karadzica Street, which we have already mentioned. Near that kindergarten.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You said that you saw two tanks. What you mean by that? You said "near the seafood restaurant. And then it went upwards. That's where I personally saw those two tanks." What tanks are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not tanks. Mortars, mobile mortars. Not tanks. I'm talking about mortars.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: At each time you saw these vehicles, did you see the weapons being transported firing? Did you see them fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw fire being opened, and I saw how men and women, Muslims, would go out of their homes and would chase those mortars from their streets because they said, "After this, we'll no longer have a roof above our heads. We'll no longer have any windows." And the Muslims protested when such mortars arrived in their streets.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you. Now, you said that there were two types of weapons you saw in these vehicles, mortars and anti-tank weapons. Is that all, or did you see any other type of weapons being carried?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mentioned those two types of weapons, and I said that I saw peculiar transporters, homemade transporters enclosed in tin -- enclosed by tin, and there was certain openings through which it was possible to fire and to observe. I assume that that was the reason for these openings.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, due to time restraint, I would appreciate it if you could restrict your answer to my question. Did you observe the direction towards which these weapons fired?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards Trebevic, towards the Serbian positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was it always the case that these weapons fired towards Trebevic, or were there other positions the weapons fired at, apart from Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Only in the direction of Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you observe tracer bullets? Do you know what tracer bullets are?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just in order to clarify, Ms. Mahindaratne, you put two questions to the witness. The answer was no. The first one: Did you observe tracer bullets? And the second one, whether he knows.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will put it again to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, do you know what tracer bullets are, tracer rounds?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've never been in the army. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well. When these weapons fired towards Trebevic, did you observe return fire from Trebevic, from the Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the sirens sounded in Sarajevo, when we heard a mobile mortar firing, we would all go to the basement. We'd take shelter. But I saw when fire was opened from an anti-aircraft -- from a mortar. It was a burst of fire directed at the Serbian side. And this mobile mortar would immediately go into another street and continue in this manner. And after about ten minutes, there would be a response and shells would start falling. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So you did see the response, to use your own words, the retaliation from the Serb side. You watched shelling, return fire from the Serb side, from Trebevic in response to this fire.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see it. I heard this. I felt it. But I couldn't observe this because I was in the basement, or in my flat.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, my question to you was: When these --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I withdraw that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your testimony was that you saw these mobile mortars and anti-tank weapons fire towards Trebevic. My question to you was: Did you see fire returning from Trebevic in response to those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, objection. The witness has answered and gave very precise information as to the locations, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, at the very end of a rather relatively long answer the witness said, "And after about ten minutes, there would be a response and the shells would start falling."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. He goes on to say that he never saw, because he went into the basement. If I -- it's at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that the answer you had in mind? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: He said, "I didn't see. I heard this. I felt it. But I couldn't observe this because I was in the basement, or in my flat."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't that what the witness said, that there was return fire but that he didn't see it but that he did hear it or --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I clarify, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please clarify the issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, is it your position that you did not see fire from Trebevic in response to the rounds of fire from the mobile mortars but you only heard it from the basement? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was it the case that every time you saw these mobile weapons you were by your house so that you could go into your basement?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President. I'm going to ask the witness to leave because I want to say something.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll answer this question though. I wasn't always in -- I wasn't always able to enter my own basement, but I would go into other people's basements, the basement of other people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin. The witness answered the question. Of course we have to -- just for time constraints, if we ask the witness to leave this courtroom, first all the curtains have to be pulled down. So if it's not necessary -- I don't know whether you persist to your --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I insist, because the witness answered an initial question very clearly, a question about the places where he saw these weapons. He answered it very clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Is sought. Ms. Mahindaratne, could you please respond. Mr. Piletta-Zanin says that in a previous answer the witness was quite precise in respect of what you're asking him now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in the interest of time, I will just withdraw that last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, wasn't there ever an instance where you saw these mortars and you did not have the opportunity to go into a basement after such weapons had fired?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said I was present when fire was opened and also when I saw them driving by, and on such occasions I didn't go into basements. I only went into the basement when they fired. It wasn't dangerous when they were moving around town. It was only dangerous when they opened fire. In such cases there would always be a response -- there would usually be a response from the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My question to you was --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I withdraw that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You stated that this was done when, to use your own words at page 17154, when there were parliamentarians from different states, from different countries, or journalists from different states visiting Bosnia, this was done. This was your testimony. Were -- are you personally aware of or were you personally privy to such an instance when there was firing from a mobile mortar, when a parliamentarian or a journalist was visiting Sarajevo? Or was the basis of your answer just rumours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not just my answer. All the citizens of Sarajevo would provide you with the same answer, regardless of their ethnic characteristics.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, if I may interrupt you. My question to you was: Were you personally privy to such an instance? Did you see with your own eyes or were you personally involved in such a situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did. I did. Not just myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think the witness was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... The witness told us what other people would respond to that question, and Ms. Mahindaratne was perfectly entitled to interrupt that type of answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have -- first then have to wait until the interpretation has been --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please, since it was not translated, repeat your answer to the last question put to you. And perhaps, Ms. Mahindaratne, you will first repeat the question as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You said you were personally privy to such an instance. When was that? Can you give the year and the month?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you the month, but it was in 1992, 1993, and 1994 for sure. I, just like all the other citizens, remained at home when parliamentary members arrived because on such occasions, it was expected that there would be firing in the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Which parliamentary members are you referring to? From which state? Are you referring to a particular incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But as -- in general, I want to say that whenever anyone visited Sarajevo, it seemed necessary to create a wartime atmosphere so that the visitors could gain an image of Sarajevo which was the image that was presented to the world.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you identify a particular situation like that? Can you refer to a specific situation, or can you only refer to it in general terms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. There were many such situations. They occurred very frequently. Whenever a foreign delegation came, new journalists, cameramen --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Just let me interrupt you. I'm asking you to identify a specific instance. Perhaps referring to the parliamentarians or journalists. Can you identify them? You said there were many situations. Can you refer to one such situation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you're asking me about one such situation, it's difficult for me to single out one particular situation. I'm telling you that this was a frequent event in Sarajevo. The mortars would always be placed in the streets to provoke a Serbian attack when foreign journalists and foreign delegations came to Sarajevo. I can't now tell you which foreign delegation. I'd need to prepare for such an answer, find out when certain people came. But as a rule, the citizens would not leave their homes when the media informed that there were visits because they knew that there would be trouble.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Moving on to another area. You testified about digging trenches below the transit road of the Jewish cemetery.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you testified that you did not volunteer to dig at the tunnel you claim some others were digging because you did not have boots.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Were you asked to dig in the tunnel and did you refuse, or is it that you merely did not volunteer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as digging the tunnel to the Jewish chapel is concerned, volunteers were requested to do this, and in return they would be given one day of leave. I didn't volunteer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So how do you reconcile that testimony with your previous position that digging trenches was forced labour and when you were specifically questioned as to whether you ever refused, you stated that refusal would be suicide? How do you reconcile these two contradictory positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those two positions are not contradictory. I appeared -- I turned up to dig trenches, but they asked for volunteers from our group. I apologise. I touched something here. But we continued digging. I haven't contradicted myself. I had to dig. I said that I was by my own freedom and my own life. That's not a contradiction. I just did not volunteer to dig the tunnel, but I dug trenches next to the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You testified that a soldier told you about the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... When was this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was towards the end of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you identify the soldier, his name or rank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was an ordinary soldier, and I don't know what his name was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You testified that schools were being used as military facilities, and you used the word "schools" in the plural.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you testified about seeing one such school. I'm referring to testimony at page 17162, where you said that it was close to the Egyptian SFOR forces, their position or their base.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Near the Egyptian forces. I said the command of the 10th Mountain Brigade was there, but the army was about 300 metres further up in a primary school. We left that school to go and dig trenches. There were military quarters there. The soldiers could sleep there. And that is the school. That's where the 10th Mountain Brigade was. It was like a small military barracks. And in other schools, Milisa Oberlica [phoen] Street on the other side of Sedrenik, we also left the primary school to go and dig. And I know that the army was there because in the hall of that school there were photographs of soldiers who had been killed. It was -- there was a catering school near the brewery, and there were other schools which were also used, and universities too, and they were used by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When you say the school you referred to, and your words were "that's where the 10th Mountain Brigade was," is that the place where you were held as a hostage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was a hostage in the yard, in the yard in front of my building, up until 4.00 in the afternoon. It was in front of my windows. And then the four of us Serbs were transferred to Caco's command through the Bistrik Street, taken to that location near the military barracks, next to the military barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, your testimony was that you were held at the command of the 10th Mountain Brigade and that's where you observed weapons. Now, here, too, you said the school you're referring to is -- to use your word "that's where the 10th Mountain Brigade was." Can you please explain. What is the characterisation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, are you referring to page 33, line 8?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Page 32, line 19, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a different --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Line 22, Mr. President. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I can assist you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Line 22?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The words were "the soldiers could sleep there and that is the school -- that's where the 10th Mountain Brigade was. It was like a small military barracks."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please read page 33, line 7 and 8 and see whether there's really much of contradiction.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I just get a clarification, Mr. President, from the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may seek a clarification. And that will be your last question before the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, the yard in which you were held hostage, was it the same building at which the 10th Mountain Brigade was, that is, the school you're referring to? Or was it a different building? When you say "yard," could you be a little bit more precise.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And then you'll have another 15 minutes, not more, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, would this be a time where you could address the Chamber? But before giving you an opportunity to do so, I would like to ask the Prosecution and draw the attention of Defence to the following issue: Under Rule 94 bis(B), the Prosecution is expected to file a motion and has got 30 days to do that once an expert report has been filed. Because of the very late filing, 15th of January, the report of the psychiatrist Dr. Kuljic and only today the report of a demographer, it will be very difficult for the Prosecution to -- if the Prosecution would take 30 days, then this would cause major problems. It's -- where the Defence always insisted on receiving timely reports, one could wonder what the consequences of this late filing should be. But I invite the Prosecution to let us know as soon as possible when it thinks it could file a notice and according to Rule 94 bis, and then - that would be the second step - to indicate how much time they would still need to prepare for cross-examination. In this respect, I ask the attention of the Defence for the following, that as I am well aware, Dr. Kuljic is scheduled quite early in your row of expert witnesses, and it was only on the 15th of January that his report was filed. That was over two weeks ago. So the Defence should be prepared to reschedule in order to allow the Prosecution to prepare for cross-examination if they would need more time. Having said this, Mr. Ierace, I invite you to make the submissions you would like to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity, Mr. President. Firstly, in relation to Dr. Kuljic, you may not have yet seen a filing today by the Prosecution in which we indicated that we would require three hours cross-examination for Dr. Kuljic. I have not yet seen the demographic report that you indicated was filed today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least, I got it on my desk today.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: We'll respond to that very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps I could start with today's filing from the Defence, entitled "Defence's submission," with the additional information and request. That document initially refers to the anticipated evidence of -- by Mr. Milan Kunjadic. At paragraph 5, the submission notes that he visited sites of the alleged incidents, which were available to the Defence. And on those sites, he performed observations, recordings, and measurements. In his report, Mr. Kunjadic said that he visited the sites - I took it to mean all of the sites - there is no reference to any recordings or measurements or indeed observations. The Prosecution requests that we be provided with the recordings, measurements, and a summary of the relevant observations. That's the first request. Moving on to the second part of that filing that relates to the prospective testimony of the accused and effectively requests that the Trial Chamber reconsider its earlier decision. It does not appear to refer to any fresh matters. It's my submission that the Defence is disentitled to invite the Trial Chamber to reconsider an earlier decision unless there are some fresh matters. Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this the part of a filing of today?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At which it is -- or is it the earlier filing?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I haven't seen it yet, so I can't -- I can't either confirm or deny that this filing exists. But you've drawn our attention to it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'm grateful to the Defence for having made this filing in the English language. It enables us to respond more quickly. So, Mr. President, the -- to save time, might I simply orally indicate the position of the Prosecution, which is that there's no fresh material, and the invitation should not be entertained. More importantly, the Defence still has not filed its exhibit list or given an indication of the time that the accused would take in chief should he be called, in spite of the specific requirement made by you of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask you, Mr. Ierace, and I'm also addressing the Defence. Am I correct in my understanding that there was an initial time indication in your witness list that has been filed and on which the accused appeared provisionally as a witness? Am I correct it's something like -- was 12 hours? Or was that -- am I mistaking now?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at this very moment I am unable to check if that is the time. But if your memory serves you well, if you say it's 12 hours, then it is. I will check, in any case. At this very moment, I cannot say for certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid that --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to check whether I have the submission here with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am afraid that my recollection is not very reliable in this respect, so it certainly should be checked. Well, it goes -- let me not respond to this right away. Let's Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 18844 to 18854. first look at the submission. On the other hand, I think that the Chamber has made it quite clear that decisions, as they are, stand and that whatever request for reconsideration is made, that the parties should meet whatever they're required to meet according to those decisions. But I'll not further respond on this at this very moment. The second issue is the facts on which Dr. Kunjadic relies. If the sources -- the sources of fact are not transparent, then one of the requirements the Chamber has expressed might not be met, and that could have as a consequence that less or no weight is attached to what the expert tells us. So, therefore, the greater the transparency, the better the Chamber is able to assess the probative value of an expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in relation to the requirement that a list of exhibits be filed for the accused. On the 23rd of January, you made it clear that the seven-day rule applies. That period has expired. They were reminded -- the Defence was reminded on Friday night. We are now perhaps two days off the calling of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps we are. But if I look at the schedule, it seem that no room has been reserved for that. And if the Defence has no intention to call the accused before the appearance of Professor Cavoski as an expert witness, I think it would be better to say that right away. And if it still intends to do so, then it's not fully comprehensible how such a schedule could be submitted to the Chamber, especially since the seven-day rule would almost impossibly be obeyed by the Defence if they were to call the accused by the end of this week. And perhaps it's not always possible, but it would be impossible. So I don't know whether the Defence want to express themselves on that. But if not, I take it that the accused will not testify and we'll then see what happens. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, in part from making gestures that are not very much comprehensible, and apart from offering a smile to the Chamber, which certainly does not assist in the work the Chamber has to perform, could you express yourself on behalf of the Defence. I'll ask lead counsel, Ms. Pilipovic -- I'll ask lead counsel, Ms. Pilipovic, whether she could express herself on behalf of the Defence or if she's unable to do so. Could you solve one of the puzzles you are putting on the table of the Chamber at this very moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in accordance with the decision of your Chamber that if the general decides to testify, that he can only testify after the fact witnesses and not expert witnesses. In accordance with this, we have compiled a schedule for this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... That was he should testify before the expert witnesses, which is not exactly the same. And I explained it several times, that it would not under all circumstances, meet after the last witness of fact, because we know that some witnesses of fact might appear later because of, well, I would say rather technical reasons where the Chamber has tried to assist the Defence as good as it could in order to make sure that these witnesses -- nevertheless, the late access to these witnesses or the late request for assistance to the Chamber that they would nevertheless appear for the Defence, since the Chamber considers it of great importance that witnesses for the Defence could appear. But I see that -- and I'm just asking you directly. It's on Tuesday that the last witness of fact on the list is indicated, whereas on Wednesday the first expert witness is scheduled. May we take it, then, that it's not your intention to call General Galic between Tuesday and Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. In accordance with your decision. In our submission that you received this morning, the Defence presented its' decision in relation to the testimony of General Galic and your decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. We'll then look at that. And that's, at least, then clear. Has the Prosecution received that submission, I take it? Yes. So then we'll also read it. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, to be perfectly clear on this, is the Defence saying that they will not be calling the accused this week for whatever reason?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you respond to that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have stated in relation to the decision of the Chamber and bearing in mind that the Chamber refused the certificate for appeal in such a decision. In accordance with this decision, the Defence has compiled a schedule of the witnesses for this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The certificate for appeal is not granted, as the Defence was aware of, I take it. It has been orally been announced. I saw the last draft, I think this morning, so it will be signed soon. Yes. I will first read what you have written down. But could you please then -- knowing that the certificate has not been granted, is the answer to the Prosecution that you do not call General Galic this week? Because that's what they asked.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in the course of this week. We have presented our position in the submission delivered this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you are free to call the accused at a later stage in accordance with the position you've taken earlier, or is that -- yes. Okay. That's clear that -- Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin -- Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just before we leave that topic, having regard to your last observation: "I take it that you are free to call the accused at a later stage in accordance with the position you've taken earlier." My --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. That you are free -- that you feel free, I think I said, or at least that's what I intended to say. That the Defence reserves its position to call General Galic at a time -- at a time different from the time the Chamber indicated in its decision when he would have to be called. That's what I -- let me -- that's at least how I understood you, Ms. Pilipovic. So the Defence differs from what the Chamber has decided and expresses its freedom to call General Galic at a time different from what the Chamber has decided. That's how I understand your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Your Honour. Precisely in accordance with what I have already stated, the Defence in its submission has requested for the Trial Chamber to reconsider its decision and allow the general, Stanislav Galic, is able to testify at any point during the Defence case in accordance with the Rules of Procedure and Evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is at least in accordance with your interpretation of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: But Mr. President, if I could just clarify my understanding of the -- of the order of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: As I understand it, it is that if the Defence elects to not call the accused at the end of its list of witnesses of fact and before it calls its first expert witness, it forfeits the opportunity to call him at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, what forfeiture will be the consequence of it is the Chamber ordered the Defence, if they wanted to call General Galic as a witness, to do it prior to examining their first expert witness. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And they could re-call him, the accused --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if necessary. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: At a later point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So that if they don't call the accused this week, that is, at the end of witnesses of fact, they cannot call the accused. I'd be grateful for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have not seen any document, although it was announced that it's on my desk downstairs, to reconsider that -- that decision, to -- that the Chamber reconsiders that decision. So I think it would be unwise to -- to say anything about it before I've read that submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I did not seek to call upon the Trial Chamber to rule -- to give its decision in respect of the yet unseen filing today, but rather, simply to clarify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You want a further clarification from the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the decision is taken. The decision is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So let's leave that. As you may know Court sometimes deliver a decision and do not comment on their own decisions any more even if requested to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Understood, Mr. President. The next issue concerning the expert witness Mr. Radinovic. At the commencement of today's session, the Prosecution was handed a letter with some attachments. The letter is from the Defence and states in effect that, pursuant to the Trial Chamber's order, it now provides to the Prosecution notes made by Professor Radinovic about conversation he had with some persons in preparation of his report. Mr. President, thereafter -- as I've said, there are a number of annexes -- one is a typed document, if I could hold it up, which -- in which some paragraphs are illegible because of a black blob. I don't know whether the Defence has a better copy. Thereafter are a number of separate annexes all in note form in B/C/S, as is the annex referred to earlier that's also in B/C/S. With the assistance of a language assistant knowledgeable in B/C/S, we have looked at these documents in the preliminary fashion. We note that some pages appear to be missing, some other matters of the like. I won't take up time now with that. We will forward a letter to the Defence requesting that they check that we have all intended pages. But we do note this: That the notes purport to be made as a result of conversations with certain persons. Some of those persons are identified, seemingly by their surname, others by a colloquial name. We're not told what the proper name is. Even so, it appears that two of the persons that the experts spoke to and on which he relies for his report include witnesses who the Defence proposed to call, no longer does, senior subordinates of the accused. One appears to be an interview with a witness who was called last week. And this is the first we have seen those notes. And it appears that, at least one more is a witness who has given evidence, DP36. There may be others. Mr. President, in my respectful submission, this is most improper, that the Prosecution be given these notes after the relevant witnesses have given their evidence so that the Prosecution does not have an opportunity to cross-examine those witnesses as to the reliability of the information they gave the expert. Secondly, it is equally improper for the expert to base his opinion in part on conversations he has had with witnesses who have not been offered for cross-examination. I refer in particular to the witnesses who were on the Defence witness list and have been dropped. That being the case, the Prosecution would be grateful if the Trial Chamber would reconsider its position in relation to the admissibility of that report, since it has been formally admitted as a result of an earlier decision of the Trial Chamber. Mr. President, today's filing, you will see in due course, also refers to Professor Radinovic's report. And this is said at paragraph 17, by way of reason as to why the time made available to the Trial Chamber for the Defence to examine him in chief should be significantly extended, paragraph 17: "Having in mind that if Defence planned possibly to admit the documents of ABiH combat units through this expert witness, which documents are not included in --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel slow down when reading, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will slow down. "To admit the documents of ABiH combat units through this expert witness, which documents are not included in expert's statement, although expert is familiar with these documents." It, therefore, appears that the Defence intends to tender, so it would seem, perhaps through this witness, material which is not referred to in his report. The understanding that the Prosecution was given by the Trial Chamber when preparing its own expert reports was that the reports had to be comprehensive and more or less speak independently as to how the opinions were arrived at, including the basis for those opinions. It should all be apparent within the report, or at least in material which has been disclosed to the Defence and identified in the report. Mr. President, this concerns the Prosecution, that it seems that at least in the case of this expert, who is to be called on one issue and then once he's in the witness box with no prior notice to the Prosecution, he's to be used for very different issue, in other words, to get in documents.
